goals: Compute a 95% confidence interval for a mean
Explain how sample size changes the width
why: A point estimate without uncertainty is half an answer. "Conversion rose 2%" is very different from "2% ± 3%".
explain: A **confidence interval** gives a range of plausible values for an unknown quantity, such as the true average delivery time.

Recipe for a mean: estimate ± (critical value × standard error). The critical value comes from the t-distribution with n − 1 degrees of freedom: 2.776 for n = 5, 1.984 for n = 100, approaching **1.96** (≈ 2) for large samples.
Correct interpretation: if we repeated the sampling many times, **95% of the intervals built this way would contain the true value**. Think of a fishing net: 95% of the nets we throw catch the fish.
Wider intervals come from more variability or smaller samples. More data narrows them.

formula.plain: Sample mean plus or minus about two standard errors.

example.title: Average delivery time (large sample)
steps: n = 100 deliveries, mean 52 min, SD 10 min
t critical value (99 degrees of freedom) = 1.984, close to 1.96 → margin = 1.98 min
example.result: "About 52 minutes, 95% CI roughly 50 to 54." More confidence costs width; to halve the width you need 4× the sample (400 deliveries).

mistakes: Saying "there is a 95% probability the true mean is in this interval" (a common but technically wrong reading of a frequentist CI).
Confusing a CI for the mean with the range of individual values.
takeaways: Always report uncertainty with an estimate

practice.code:
from scipy import stats
mean, sd, n = 52, 10, 100
se = sd / n**0.5
for conf in [0.90, 0.95, 0.99]:
    lo, hi = stats.t.interval(conf, n - 1, loc=mean, scale=se)
    print(conf, round(lo, 2), round(hi, 2))   # 0.95 → 50.02 53.98

check.why: More data reduces the standard error.
